events.text: The husk lets go. I am painting an imagined open sweet-chestnut husk and two warm nuts on blue linen, inspired by the Woodland Trust sweet-chestnut guide. Goal: broad filled planes first, then sparse fine spines and one compact reflection. Begin with long quiet cloth washes.
The long washes leave pale horizontal gaps. Bridge those gaps with broad blue neighbors before placing the green husk; keep the upper field quiet.
The bridge washes closed the cream gaps while keeping soft bands. Place a low soft contact and broad green husk planes; the blue field stays open above.
The first husk is a hollow ring. Fill across that blue slit with pale inner lining and a warm nut; broad crossing passes should join the forms before any spines.
The crossing closed the blue hole and seated the nut. Its warm face needs a lighter side; first establish the second nut lower right with a clear blue gap between them.
Both nuts are filled and separated by blue. The seated nut has a darker right turn. Add a long unequal leaf above the loose nut, then a pale inner lip to make the husk opening explicit.
The pale lip reads as an opening, but crown and leaf remain angular. Use sampled curved shoulder gestures and a narrow dark split; preserve broad midvalues for later sparse spines.
The sampled green shoulder rounds the left side, though the old crown peak remains. The split became a heavy dark bar; shorten it with a pale neighbor and establish the nuts’ dull attachment scars.
The dark split is shorter but still has raised ends. Attachment scars now distinguish the nuts. Warm sampled planes will turn their lit sides, followed by one long leaf midrib.
Warm side gestures read as patches rather than smooth shell gradients; keep that irregularity for now. Try four fine uneven spines on the upper-left husk edge and judge their scale before repeating.
The first fine spines stay subordinate at whole view and taper cleanly close up. Extend their uneven rhythm around the crown with slightly lighter tips, leaving gaps rather than a comb.
Loaded fine tips are clearer than the first thin pass. Continue around the left/lower edge with unequal lengths and darker bases; avoid filling every interval.
The lower tips now break the smooth outline. Leave a quieter interval beneath the nut and add only four right-side tips so the pale opening remains dominant.
The perimeter is readable without becoming a dense comb. Interior spines should be shorter and cross the broad green planes at varied angles, keeping the pale lining clear.
Short interior tips are subtle at whole view, which keeps the shell planes broad. Add a few lower facing tips, then stop spine work and develop the leaf’s structure.
The leaf is still a smooth strap. Four angled veins can suggest its folded sides without outlining the entire edge.
The upper veins read at whole view but have raised joins. Keep the lower veins darker, and add only two small edge teeth to interrupt the strap silhouette.
The first edge teeth stayed inside the broad leaf and barely changed its outline. Place two farther out, then connect the leaf base with a thin warm petiole.
The farther teeth change the silhouette but leave small angular loops. Fill their bases with green neighbors, and broaden the seated nut’s lit plane to reduce its central notch.
The seated nut’s light is broader; repeat that correction on the loose nut and taper both pointed crowns. Keep the right sides dark for a clear turn.
The loose nut is warmer but still patchy. Its floor contact is weaker than the husk’s; use soft watercolor beneath it and a short restrained oil accent only where it touches.
Inspect the lower nut and its new contact closely before changing its scar or highlight.

The lower review shows a joined soft contact, a dull scar, and raised vertical patching in the loose nut; crown is cropped from this view. Add sparse scar grain and two warmer shell neighbors, keeping the reflection for later.
The dark split still reads as a short bar. Reduce its upper end with a broad green neighbor and soften the pale lining’s left join, judging color separately from relief.
The split is quieter in color, with raised remnants still visible close up. Prepare a warm light under the seated nut’s focal reflection and keep the loose nut’s reflection longer but duller.
The warm underlight is visible without being white. Test the focal reflection alone: a short loaded mark on the seated nut’s upper-left shoulder.

The compact reflection holds at whole view. Final refinement: quiet the loose nut’s long underlight, a raised leaf vein join, and the pale lower lining. Stop when those relationships hold rather than adding more spines.

Finished at 100 completed marks. Broad overlaps closed the early blue hole; fine loaded spines taper without filling every interval, two warm nuts stay separated by blue, and one compact seated-nut reflection holds focus. Final neighbors quieted color but left raised joins. Faceted crown, sparse serrations, patchy shell planes and regular bristles remain. Stop here: further covering chiefly builds relief, so the count is not padded.

creation.method: 100 animated watercolor/oil strokes in 26 batches of 1–4, selected after settled whole-and-close screenshots; no whole score prepared in advance.
creation.evidence: 26 whole/close review boundaries. Initial4 whole screenshot was viewed but not saved; close4 and all25 subsequent pairs saved. Initial4 framing adjusted after scroll; rectangle read preceded scroll settling, screenshot itself showed whole canvas. Lower84 additional close review showed loose-nut contact but cropped crown and right edge.
creation.notes: 54 live notes/camera moments. Live from this laptop confirmed before opening. Ended public feed exactly matched raw100 strokes and54 events before this metadata addition. No retrospective replay events added.
creation.finish: Single97 reflection inspected alone;98–100 final refinement followed by deliberate paired review. Stop100 as additional covers chiefly build relief; no padding toward112.
